The first thing that comes to mind is a memory of rain. Not the dramatic kind, but a slow, gray drizzle that blurs the edges of houses and turns the street into a mirror. I was standing at the window, watching a man walk his dog, and the dog kept stopping to sniff the wet pavement as if the rain had left secrets there. The man didn’t rush; he let the dog linger. Something about that tiny patience felt like a form of love. I think about that moment more than I should, maybe because it asked nothing of me.

Now the page is open and I am supposed to fill it. The cursor blinks like a metronome, steady and indifferent. I could write about anything—there is no wrong answer—but that freedom is its own kind of cage. If I choose a memory, which one? If I invent a story, who gets to speak? The easiest thing is to describe the room: the hum of the refrigerator, the stack of books with cracked spines, the faint smell of coffee going stale. But description is just a way of stalling. Eventually, even the dust on the windowsill becomes a character with a past.

Loneliness has a texture. It feels like the inside of a wool coat against bare skin—warm, but scratchy enough to remind you it’s there. I used to think loneliness was empty, but it’s actually crowded with all the versions of yourself you’ve outgrown. They sit in the corners, polite and out of fashion, waiting to be acknowledged. Sometimes I wave at them. Other times I pretend they are furniture. The strange part is that they don’t mind. They know they are part of the architecture now. They know the house is still standing because they hold it all up.

There is a theory that every story is about a character wanting something and failing to get it. I think about that when I want coffee but the pot is empty. The wanting is small, the failure manageable, but the structure holds. I stand in the kitchen, staring at the glass carafe, and for a second I am a protagonist in a tragedy of minor inconvenience. Then I fill the kettle, and the story becomes about water changing state. Heat, steam, the whistle. Maybe that’s the secret: shift the desire, and the plot resolves itself. Or maybe not. Maybe the plot simply waits.

Words are slippery. You think you’ve caught one—say, the word ‘home’—but it wriggles free and becomes a smell, a stair creak, a particular shade of yellow on a kitchen wall. I have learned not to trust nouns. They pretend to be solid, but they are really doors. Open one and you fall into a hallway of associations. Home becomes the sound of my mother’s keys in the lock. Home becomes the cold side of the pillow. Home becomes a place I can’t return to because it exists only in the act of remembering. Still, I keep opening doors.

Sometimes I think about all the people who have ever written a thousand words and then deleted them. There must be millions. A silent army of almost-writers, their sentences rising like vapor and vanishing before anyone could read them. Is that sad? I don’t know. Maybe it’s generous. Not every thought needs an audience. Some thoughts are like seeds that need to stay buried. Others are like boats made of paper—meant to float for a moment, then dissolve. I write this and wonder which kind it is. The truth: I won’t know until I stop.

The clock on the wall has stopped at 3:07. It has been 3:07 for as long as I can remember, which means the clock is either broken or very patient. I prefer to think it’s patient. It is waiting for the right moment to resume, and that moment is not now. I understand. There are days when I too feel stopped, stuck at a particular hour, watching the rest of the world move forward in a blur. But maybe being stopped is not the same as being broken. Maybe it’s a form of attention. The clock is paying attention to 3:07, and I am paying attention to the clock.

Maybe the reason I write is to find out what I think. Not what I know—knowing is too finished, too polished—but what I am thinking in the moment of typing, before the thought has time to harden into opinion. There is a small, bright interval between the brain and the fingers, and in that gap, truth sometimes slips through. I try not to edit it away. Later, I can be smart. Later, I can be coherent. For now, I want the raw material: the hesitation, the repetition, the sentence that starts one way and ends somewhere else entirely. That is where the living happens.

One thousand words is both a lot and not enough. It is enough to sketch a face but not to know the person. Enough to describe a room but not the life lived inside it. Enough to begin a thought and follow it around a corner, but not to reach the end of the street. I could use these remaining words to tell you something true: I am afraid of being forgotten, and also afraid of being seen. Both things live in the same breath. I write because it is the only way I know to be invisible and present at the same time. You are reading this, so maybe it works.

I used to think that if I could just find the right words, the world would make sense. Now I know the words don’t make sense; they just keep me company. They sit beside me in the dark, small and warm, like a candle that doesn’t mind the wind. They do not ask me to be better. They only ask me to keep going. So here is my thousandth word: quietly stay, and listen, and then begin again.
